bmt-2018-spring-power-01a.title: Compare the neighbors of vertex 1
bmt-2018-spring-power-01a.body:
In the left graph the edges are $1$-$2$, $1$-$3$, $1$-$4$, $2$-$4$, $3$-$4$, so vertex $1$ is adjacent to $2$, $3$ and $4$. In the right graph the edges are $1$-$2$, $1$-$4$, $2$-$3$, $2$-$4$, $3$-$4$, so vertex $1$ is adjacent only to $2$ and $4$. A label-preserving map must send the neighbors of $1$ to the neighbors of $1$, so the graphs are not isomorphic.

**Answer: No**

bmt-2018-spring-power-01b.title: Count the edges
bmt-2018-spring-power-01b.body:
The left graph has the $9$ edges $1$-$2$, $1$-$4$, $2$-$3$, $2$-$5$, $2$-$6$, $3$-$4$, $3$-$5$, $4$-$5$, $5$-$6$. The right graph has $10$ edges: $1$-$2$, $1$-$4$, $2$-$3$, $2$-$5$, $2$-$6$, $3$-$4$, $3$-$5$, $3$-$6$, $4$-$6$, $5$-$6$. Isomorphic graphs have the same number of edges, so they are not isomorphic.

**Answer: No**

bmt-2018-spring-power-01c.title: Compare the edge lists
bmt-2018-spring-power-01c.body:
Both graphs have the $12$ edges $1$-$6$, $1$-$7$, $1$-$8$, $2$-$5$, $2$-$7$, $2$-$8$, $3$-$5$, $3$-$6$, $3$-$8$, $4$-$5$, $4$-$6$, $4$-$7$ (each is the cube graph, drawn differently). Since the labeled edge sets coincide, the identity map on labels is an isomorphism.

**Answer: Yes**

bmt-2018-spring-power-02.title: Inspect the tree
bmt-2018-spring-power-02.body:
The graph is a tree with edges $1$-$2$, $2$-$3$, $3$-$5$, $2$-$4$, $2$-$6$, $6$-$7$. Vertex $2$ has branches ending at $1$, $4$, $5$ (through $3$) and $7$ (through $6$). A longest path joins the two longest branches: the branch through $3$ to $5$ (length $2$ from vertex $2$) and the branch through $6$ to $7$ (length $2$). The other branches have length $1$.

So the longest path is $7,6,2,3,5$ (or reversed), with $4$ edges.

**Answer: $7,6,2,3,5$**

bmt-2018-spring-power-03a.title: Proof
bmt-2018-spring-power-03a.body: By definition, for any two vertices $u,v$ of a tree there is exactly one path from $u$ to $v$. In particular there is a path between any two vertices, which is the definition of connected. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2018-spring-power-03b.title: Proof
bmt-2018-spring-power-03b.body: Suppose a tree contained a cycle $v_1,\dots,v_k$ with $k\ge3$. Then $v_1$ and $v_k$ are neighbors, so $(v_1,v_k)$ is a path from $v_1$ to $v_k$ with $2$ vertices. But $v_1,v_2,\dots,v_k$ is also a path from $v_1$ to $v_k$, with $k\ge3$ vertices. These are two different paths between the same pair of vertices, contradicting the definition of a tree. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2018-spring-power-04.title: Endpoints of a longest path
bmt-2018-spring-power-04.body:
Let $T$ be a tree and let $v_0,v_1,\dots,v_k$ be a longest path in $T$ ($k\ge1$ since $T$ has at least two vertices and is connected). We show $v_0$ is a leaf. Suppose $v_0$ has a neighbor $w\ne v_1$.

- If $w$ is not on the path, then $w,v_0,v_1,\dots,v_k$ is a longer path, a contradiction.
- If $w=v_j$ for some $j\ge2$, then $v_0,v_1,\dots,v_j$ is a cycle (its first and last vertices are neighbors and it has at least $3$ vertices), contradicting problem 3(b).

So $v_0$ has the single neighbor $v_1$, hence is a leaf. The same argument for $v_k$ shows it is a leaf, and $v_0\ne v_k$. So there are at least two leaves. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2018-spring-power-05.title: Proof
bmt-2018-spring-power-05.body: Let $\ell$ be a leaf of $T$ and let $T'=T-\ell$, which has $n-1\ge2$ vertices. Take two vertices $u,v\ne\ell$ and let $p$ be the unique path from $u$ to $v$ in $T$. An interior vertex of a path has two different neighbors on the path, so it has degree at least $2$; since $\ell$ has degree $1$, $\ell$ is not an interior vertex of $p$, and it is not an endpoint, so $p$ avoids $\ell$ and is a path in $T'$. Any path from $u$ to $v$ in $T'$ is also a path in $T$, hence equals $p$. So there is exactly one path in $T'$ between any two vertices: $T'$ is a tree. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2018-spring-power-06.title: Classify by shape
bmt-2018-spring-power-06.body:
A tree on $4$ vertices has $3$ edges and at least $2$ leaves, so it is either a star (one vertex adjacent to the other three) or a path through all four vertices.

- **Stars:** the center can be any of the $4$ labels: $4$ trees.
- **Paths:** a path is an ordering of $1,2,3,4$, and an ordering and its reverse give the same tree: $\frac{4!}2=12$ trees. Listing the orderings with first entry smaller than the last: $1234,1243,1324,1342,1423,1432,2134,2143,2314,2413,3124,3214$.

Total $4+12=16$. The three given trees are the paths $1234$ and $1324$ and the star centered at $2$.

bmt-2018-spring-power-07.title: Induction on the number of vertices
bmt-2018-spring-power-07.body:
We show: while the current graph is a tree with at least $3$ vertices, one step of the algorithm can be performed and leaves a tree with one fewer vertex.

- By problem 4 the tree has at least two leaves, so a leaf with the largest label exists (labels are distinct).
- A leaf has exactly one neighbor, so there is exactly one label to write down.
- Deleting the leaf and its edge leaves a tree on one fewer vertex, which is still at least $2$ (problem 5).

Each step removes one vertex, so after $n-2$ steps exactly two vertices remain; the tree on two vertices has just one edge (the two vertices are connected by the unique path, which is that edge). So the algorithm never gets stuck and ends with a single edge. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2018-spring-power-08a.title: Run the algorithm
bmt-2018-spring-power-08a.body:
Apply the algorithm (largest leaf first):

- remove leaf $8$, write $6$
- remove leaf $7$, write $4$
- remove leaf $6$, write $5$
- remove leaf $5$, write $1$
- remove leaf $4$, write $1$
- remove leaf $3$, write $1$

The remaining edge is $1$-$2$.

**Answer: $6, 4, 5, 1, 1, 1$**

bmt-2018-spring-power-08b.title: Run the algorithm
bmt-2018-spring-power-08b.body:
Apply the algorithm (largest leaf first):

- remove leaf $8$, write $2$
- remove leaf $3$, write $7$
- remove leaf $7$, write $6$
- remove leaf $6$, write $5$
- remove leaf $2$, write $5$
- remove leaf $5$, write $4$

The remaining edge is $1$-$4$.

**Answer: $2, 7, 6, 5, 5, 4$**

bmt-2018-spring-power-08c.title: Run the algorithm
bmt-2018-spring-power-08c.body:
Apply the algorithm (largest leaf first):

- remove leaf $7$, write $6$
- remove leaf $6$, write $4$
- remove leaf $5$, write $4$
- remove leaf $4$, write $2$
- remove leaf $3$, write $1$

The remaining edge is $1$-$2$.

**Answer: $6, 4, 4, 2, 1$**

bmt-2018-spring-power-09.title: Proof
bmt-2018-spring-power-09.body: While the current tree has at least $3$ vertices, it has at least two leaves (problem 4). Vertex $1$ has the smallest label, so if $1$ is a leaf, the other leaf has a larger label; hence the largest leaf is never vertex $1$. So vertex $1$ is never deleted, and it is one of the two remaining vertices at the end. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2018-spring-power-10.title: Count the edges at k
bmt-2018-spring-power-10.body:
Each of the $n-2$ steps deletes one edge, namely the edge at the leaf removed; the last remaining edge is never deleted. Let $d$ be the degree of the vertex $k$.

- Suppose $k$ is deleted at some step (as the largest leaf). At that moment it has exactly one remaining edge, so it lost its other $d-1$ edges earlier, each when its other endpoint (a leaf at that time) was deleted; each such deletion wrote down $k$. At its own deletion $k$ is not written. So $k$ appears $d-1$ times.
- Suppose $k$ is never deleted, so it is one of the two final vertices. All its edges except possibly the final edge were deleted with the other endpoint being deleted, and each wrote $k$. The final edge is not deleted, and it is one of its edges, so $d-1$ edges were deleted, and $k$ appears $d-1$ times.

In both cases $j_k=d-1$, i.e. $\deg k=j_k+1$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2018-spring-power-11.title: Stars
bmt-2018-spring-power-11.body:
**Claim.** $T$ has a constant Prüfer code if and only if $T$ is a star, i.e. some vertex $c$ is adjacent to all other vertices; then the code is $c,c,\dots,c$.

*Sufficient.* In a star with center $c$ every other vertex is a leaf adjacent to $c$. While at least $3$ vertices remain, the center has degree at least $2$, so it is not a leaf, and the largest leaf is some non-center vertex with neighbor $c$. So each of the $n-2$ steps writes $c$.

*Necessary.* Suppose the code is $c,c,\dots,c$ ($n-2$ times). By problem 10, vertex $c$ has degree $(n-2)+1=n-1$, so it is adjacent to every other vertex. These are $n-1$ edges, which is all the edges of a tree on $n$ vertices (a tree on $n$ vertices has $n-1$ edges), so $T$ is exactly the star centered at $c$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2018-spring-power-12a.title: Reverse the algorithm
bmt-2018-spring-power-12a.body:
Rebuild the tree on $8$ vertices: at each step take the largest label that is not in the rest of the code (and not yet used), and join it to the next code entry.

- join leaf $8$ to $1$
- join leaf $7$ to $1$
- join leaf $6$ to $3$
- join leaf $3$ to $2$
- join leaf $2$ to $4$
- join leaf $4$ to $5$
- finally join the two labels left over: $1$-$5$

The tree has the edges $1$-$5$, $1$-$7$, $1$-$8$, $2$-$3$, $2$-$4$, $3$-$6$, $4$-$5$.

**Answer: edges $1$-$5$, $1$-$7$, $1$-$8$, $2$-$3$, $2$-$4$, $3$-$6$, $4$-$5$**

bmt-2018-spring-power-12b.title: Reverse the algorithm
bmt-2018-spring-power-12b.body:
Rebuild the tree on $10$ vertices: at each step take the largest label that is not in the rest of the code (and not yet used), and join it to the next code entry.

- join leaf $10$ to $1$
- join leaf $9$ to $1$
- join leaf $8$ to $2$
- join leaf $7$ to $2$
- join leaf $6$ to $1$
- join leaf $5$ to $1$
- join leaf $4$ to $2$
- join leaf $3$ to $2$
- finally join the two labels left over: $1$-$2$

The tree has the edges $1$-$2$, $1$-$5$, $1$-$6$, $1$-$9$, $1$-$10$, $2$-$3$, $2$-$4$, $2$-$7$, $2$-$8$.

**Answer: edges $1$-$2$, $1$-$5$, $1$-$6$, $1$-$9$, $1$-$10$, $2$-$3$, $2$-$4$, $2$-$7$, $2$-$8$**

bmt-2018-spring-power-12c.title: Reverse the algorithm
bmt-2018-spring-power-12c.body:
Rebuild the tree on $12$ vertices: at each step take the largest label that is not in the rest of the code (and not yet used), and join it to the next code entry.

- join leaf $12$ to $6$
- join leaf $11$ to $5$
- join leaf $9$ to $4$
- join leaf $8$ to $3$
- join leaf $6$ to $1$
- join leaf $5$ to $1$
- join leaf $4$ to $7$
- join leaf $7$ to $3$
- join leaf $3$ to $1$
- join leaf $2$ to $10$
- finally join the two labels left over: $1$-$10$

The tree has the edges $1$-$3$, $1$-$5$, $1$-$6$, $1$-$10$, $2$-$10$, $3$-$7$, $3$-$8$, $4$-$7$, $4$-$9$, $5$-$11$, $6$-$12$.

**Answer: edges $1$-$3$, $1$-$5$, $1$-$6$, $1$-$10$, $2$-$10$, $3$-$7$, $3$-$8$, $4$-$7$, $4$-$9$, $5$-$11$, $6$-$12$**

bmt-2018-spring-power-13a.title: Reconstruction algorithm
bmt-2018-spring-power-13a.body:
1. Draw $n$ vertices labeled $1,\dots,n$ and write the list $L=(1,2,\dots,n)$ of unused labels.
2. If the sequence is empty, join the two labels remaining in $L$ by an edge and stop.
3. Otherwise find the largest label $\ell$ in $L$ that does not occur in the (remaining) sequence. Join $\ell$ to the first entry $s$ of the sequence by an edge.
4. Delete $\ell$ from $L$ and delete the first entry from the sequence; go to step 2.

This works because the leaves of a tree are exactly the labels that do not appear in its Prüfer code (problem 10), so $\ell$ is the leaf the encoding algorithm removed first, and its neighbor is $s$.

bmt-2018-spring-power-13b.title: The Prüfer code is a bijection
bmt-2018-spring-power-13b.body:
For any finite set $V$ of labels (totally ordered) with $|V|=n\ge2$, let $P$ map labeled trees on $V$ to sequences in $V^{n-2}$ (the Prüfer code). We prove by induction on $n$ that $P$ is a bijection; then the number of trees is $|V^{n-2}|=n^{n-2}$.

$n=2$: one tree, one (empty) sequence.

$n\ge3$: let $s=(s_1,\dots,s_{n-2})\in V^{n-2}$. The set of labels not appearing in $s$ has at least $2$ elements; let $\ell$ be its largest element.

*At most one tree.* If $P(T)=s$, then by problem 10 the leaves of $T$ are exactly the labels not occurring in $s$, so the largest leaf of $T$ is $\ell$ and its neighbor is $s_1$. Then $T-\ell$ is a tree on $V\setminus\{\ell\}$ with Prüfer code $(s_2,\dots,s_{n-2})$ (all entries lie in $V\setminus\{\ell\}$ since $\ell\notin s$), which by the induction hypothesis determines $T-\ell$ uniquely. So $T$ is that tree plus the edge $\ell s_1$.

*At least one tree.* Let $T'$ be the tree on $V\setminus\{\ell\}$ with $P(T')=(s_2,\dots,s_{n-2})$ (induction), and let $T$ be $T'$ with a new leaf $\ell$ attached to $s_1$. For $k\in V$ the degree in $T$ is $\deg_{T'}(k)+[k=s_1]$ for $k\ne\ell$, i.e. $1+\#\{i\ge2:s_i=k\}+[k=s_1]=1+\#\{i:s_i=k\}$, and $\deg_T(\ell)=1=1+\#\{i:s_i=\ell\}$. So the leaves of $T$ are exactly the labels not occurring in $s$, the largest leaf is $\ell$ with neighbor $s_1$, and after removing it we are left with $T'$ whose code is $(s_2,\dots)$; thus $P(T)=s$.

So $P$ is a bijection and there are $n^{n-2}$ labeled trees. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2018-spring-power-14a.title: Run the algorithm
bmt-2018-spring-power-14a.body:
Orient all edges away from vertex $1$ and traverse the paths from $1$ to $i=2,\dots,8$:

- $i=2$: path $1\to 2$; new edges write 1
- $i=3$: path $1\to 3$; new edges write 1
- $i=4$: path $1\to 4$; new edges write 1
- $i=5$: path $1\to 5$; new edges write 1
- $i=6$: path $1\to 5\to 6$; new edges write 5
- $i=7$: path $1\to 4\to 7$; new edges write 4
- $i=8$: path $1\to 5\to 6\to 8$; new edges write 6

**Answer: $1, 1, 1, 1, 5, 4, 6$**

bmt-2018-spring-power-14b.title: Run the algorithm
bmt-2018-spring-power-14b.body:
Orient all edges away from vertex $1$ and traverse the paths from $1$ to $i=2,\dots,8$:

- $i=2$: path $1\to 4\to 5\to 2$; new edges write 1, 4, 5
- $i=3$: path $1\to 4\to 5\to 6\to 7\to 3$; new edges write 5, 6, 7
- $i=4$: path $1\to 4$; new edges write nothing
- $i=5$: path $1\to 4\to 5$; new edges write nothing
- $i=6$: path $1\to 4\to 5\to 6$; new edges write nothing
- $i=7$: path $1\to 4\to 5\to 6\to 7$; new edges write nothing
- $i=8$: path $1\to 4\to 5\to 6\to 7\to 3\to 8$; new edges write 3

**Answer: $1, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 3$**

bmt-2018-spring-power-14c.title: Run the algorithm
bmt-2018-spring-power-14c.body:
Orient all edges away from vertex $1$ and traverse the paths from $1$ to $i=2,\dots,7$:

- $i=2$: path $1\to 2$; new edges write 1
- $i=3$: path $1\to 3$; new edges write 1
- $i=4$: path $1\to 2\to 4$; new edges write 2
- $i=5$: path $1\to 2\to 4\to 5$; new edges write 4
- $i=6$: path $1\to 2\to 4\to 6$; new edges write 4
- $i=7$: path $1\to 2\to 4\to 7$; new edges write 4

**Answer: $1, 1, 2, 4, 4, 4$**

bmt-2018-spring-power-15.title: Proof
bmt-2018-spring-power-15.body: For $i=2$ we traverse the path from vertex $1$ to vertex $2$, which has at least one edge and starts at $1$. All its edges are new, and the first edge $e$ crossed has its tail at vertex $1$ (edges are oriented away from $1$). So the first entry appended is $c(e)=1$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2018-spring-power-16.title: Each vertex appears once per child edge
bmt-2018-spring-power-16.body:
Every one of the $n-1$ edges is crossed for the first time exactly once (the traversals to $2,\dots,n$ together cover every edge, since each vertex $i$ is reached), and each time $c(e)$, the tail of $e$, is appended. So the Fleiner code lists, for every edge, its tail; the label $v$ appears exactly as often as $v$ is the tail of an edge, i.e. $v$ appears (number of neighbors of $v$ farther from $1$) times.

Hence the entries are all distinct iff every vertex has at most one edge leading away from $1$.

**Claim.** This holds iff $T$ is a path with $1$ as an end vertex.

If $T$ is a path with $1$ at one end, orienting away from $1$ gives each vertex at most one outgoing edge. Conversely, suppose each vertex has at most one outgoing edge. Starting at $1$ and following the unique outgoing edge repeatedly gives a path $1=v_0,v_1,\dots$ that ends at a vertex with no outgoing edge; every vertex of $T$ lies on a path from $1$, and at each vertex on the way only one continuation exists, so all vertices lie on this one path. So $T$ is a path starting at $1$ (vertex $1$ has one outgoing edge, so it has degree $1$: it is an end). $\blacksquare$

bmt-2018-spring-power-17.title: Induction removing the largest leaf
bmt-2018-spring-power-17.body:
We work with a tree on any finite totally ordered label set; the root is the smallest label (for the original problem it is $1$), "orient away from the root" and the Fleiner code is defined with $i$ running over the other labels in increasing order. For $n=2$ the claim is empty.

**Description of the Fleiner code.** For a non-root vertex $v$ let $\text{par}(v)$ be its parent (the tail of the edge into $v$) and $m(v)$ the smallest label in the subtree of $v$ (all vertices whose path from the root passes through $v$, including $v$). The edge into $v$ is crossed for the first time when $i=m(v)$. During the traversal for a given $i$, the new edges are exactly the edges into the vertices $v$ on the path with $m(v)=i$; these form the last part of the path (if $m(v)=i$ and $w$ is below $v$ on the path then $m(w)=i$ too), and they are appended in order from the root downward. So the Fleiner code lists $\text{par}(v)$ for all non-root $v$, sorted by the key $(m(v),\ \text{depth}(v))$ in increasing order.

**Inductive step ($n\ge3$).** Let $\ell$ be the largest leaf of $T$; $\ell$ is not the root (there are at least two leaves, and the root has the smallest label), so $\ell$ has no children, and let $p$ be its neighbor, which is its parent and the first entry of the Prüfer code. Let $T'=T-\ell$, a tree on $n-1\ge2$ vertices, with the same root. The Prüfer code of $T'$ is the Prüfer code of $T$ without its first entry.

*(1) The entry for $\ell$ is last.* For a non-root vertex $v\ne\ell$, the subtree of $v$ contains a vertex with no children, which is a leaf of $T$, so $m(v)\le$ that leaf $\le\ell$. If $m(v)=\ell$, the subtree of $v$ contains $\ell$ as its smallest label and also a leaf at most $\ell$, so that leaf is $\ell$; then $v$ is a proper ancestor of $\ell$ and has smaller depth. Hence the key of $\ell$, $(\ell,\text{depth}(\ell))$, is larger than all other keys.

*(2) Deleting $\ell$ does not change the order of the other entries.* For vertices $v$ that are not ancestors of $\ell$, nothing changes. For an ancestor $v$ of $\ell$ with $m(v)<\ell$, the minimum is attained at a vertex other than $\ell$, so $m(v)$ is unchanged. The remaining ancestors have $m(v)=\ell$; after deleting $\ell$ their keys $m'(v)$ are larger than $\ell$, hence larger than all keys of vertices with $m<\ell$ (all other vertices, by (1)), and among themselves $m'$ is non-decreasing going down the path, with ties broken by depth, so their order is unchanged; before deleting they also came after all the vertices with $m<\ell$ and in the same order among themselves.

So $F(T)=F(T')$ followed by $p$. By induction, the last $n-3$ entries of $F(T')$ are the reverse of the Prüfer code of $T'$, which is $(s_2,\dots,s_{n-2})$ reversed, and so the last $n-2$ entries of $F(T)$ are $s_{n-2},\dots,s_2$ followed by $p=s_1$: the reverse of $(s_1,\dots,s_{n-2})$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2018-spring-power-18a.title: Count Fleiner codes
